deep.reconstruction:
Context: this folio is a working draft of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Ueber die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (1854, published posthumously 1867). It corresponds to the end of Part I (§§10-12, especially the material leading into §13). The previous page drafts the improper-integral definition (§4). The next page drafts the integrability criterion with oscillations sigma and total length s (§5), and the heading of Part II: 'Ueber den Fall, wenn die Glieder der Reihe Omega nicht für jeden Argumentwerth zuletzt unendlich klein werden'.

Notation (Riemann's, filled in by me from the published text):
- Omega = A_0 + A_1 + A_2 + ..., with A_n = a_n sin(nx) + b_n cos(nx).
- F(x) = C + C'x + A_0 x^2/2 - sum_{n>=1} A_n/n^2, the formal twice-integrated series.
- lambda(x) is an auxiliary function on [b,c] such that lambda and lambda' vanish at b and c, and lambda'' is piecewise monotone (finitely many maxima and minima).

Paragraph 1. Assume that for every interval (b,c) the quantity mu^2 * Int_b^c F(x) lambda(x) cos(mu(x - xi)) dx tends to 0 as mu -> infinity. Then the coefficients a_n, b_n tend to 0. In the partial sum of the first n terms, the influence of every interval vanishes as n -> infinity, except for an arbitrarily small interval containing the point x. Hence whether Omega converges at x depends only on the behaviour of the function in an arbitrarily small neighbourhood of x. This is Riemann's localization principle (published §10, Satz III and its consequence).

Paragraph 2. Suppose instead that at isolated points this fails: the integral mu^2 Int F lambda cos mu(x - xi) dx tends to 0 only when those points lie outside the limits of integration. Then a_n, b_n do not tend to 0. That is, there is a finite bound such that, however far one goes in the series, coefficients larger than this bound still occur. This is the situation treated in Part II.

Paragraph 3 (pencil, partly illegible). The partial sum A_1 + ... + A_n is related to an integral (1/pi) Int_b^c (...) [sin((2n+1)(x-t)/2) / (2 sin((x-t)/2))] phi(t) dt. Here the Dirichlet kernel appears, and the parenthesis is presumably a second t-derivative or second-difference factor. As n -> infinity this converges to A (the value), 'whereby one obtains the above theorem'. In the published text the corresponding formula is A_0 + ... + A_n = (1/2pi) Int_b^c F(t) d^2/dt^2[ sin((2n+1)(x-t)/2) / sin((x-t)/2) ] lambda(t) dt + (terms -> 0). The underlying identity is 1/2 + sum_{k=1}^n cos(k u) = sin((2n+1)u/2) / (2 sin(u/2)).

Paragraph 4. Conclusion: if the terms of Omega tend to 0 for every x, then convergence at a given x depends only on the behaviour of the function near x. Whether the terms do tend to 0 for every x must in many cases be decided not from their expression as definite integrals (Int_b^c cos mu(x-a) lambda(x) dx for infinite mu) but in some other way. One special case deserves emphasis, where this follows directly from the nature of the function: 1) if the function does not have infinitely many maxima and minima, this is sufficient (continued on the next leaf). This corresponds to the published §13 discussion of Dirichlet-type conditions.

No actual computation is carried out on this page. It is expository drafting of theorems whose proofs appear elsewhere.
errors: No mathematical errors detectable. The statements agree with the published Habilitationsschrift.

Paragraph 2 is phrased loosely. Failure of the mu^2-integral condition at isolated points does not by itself force a_n, b_n not to tend to 0 without further argument. The published Part II handles this more carefully: coefficients tending to 0 is equivalent to a local condition holding everywhere.

The pencil formula linking the partial sum to the Dirichlet-kernel integral is fragmentary. The factor written '(...)^2' cannot be checked. In the published version it is a second derivative of the kernel multiplied by lambda(t) and F(t).

results.what: Convergence of a trigonometric series with coefficients tending to 0 at a point depends only on the behaviour of (the twice-integrated function) F in an arbitrarily small neighbourhood of that point
results.modern_name: Riemann localization principle (for general trigonometric series)

results.what: Partial sums expressed via an integral with the Dirichlet kernel sin((2n+1)u/2)/(2 sin(u/2))
results.modern_name: Dirichlet kernel representation of partial sums

results.what: If the integrals mu^2 Int F lambda cos mu(x-xi) dx fail to vanish near isolated points, the coefficients need not tend to 0; this motivates the case of terms not tending to zero everywhere
results.modern_name: Riemann's analysis of series whose terms do not tend to 0 (Part II of the Habilitationsschrift)

results.what: Finitely many maxima/minima as a sufficient condition decidable from the nature of the function

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of passages of Riemann's well-known 1854 Habilitationsschrift on trigonometric series (localization principle, Dirichlet kernel, transition to Part II). The content is fully known and credited to him. Only the draft wording and ordering are of minor philological interest.

transcription_corrections: Line 1: 'Wenn [-aber-] für jedes Grössenintervall' — the integrand reads F(x) lambda(x) cos mu(x - xi), with the factor mu^2 in front, consistent with the published Satz III.
'statt eines' in paragraph 2 is likely 'stets eine' ('es lässt sich stets eine endliche Grenze angeben').
'Die Reihe A_1+A_2+...+A_n und dem Integral' probably reads 'Die Summe A_1 + ... + A_n und das Integral (1/pi) Int_b^c ... nähern sich ... [einander]'.
'aus ihrem Ausdruck' should continue as in print: 'nicht aus ihrem Ausdruck als bestimmte Integrale'.
'verdient nun noch die eine besondere Fälle hervorzuheben zu werden' is likely 'Es verdient indess ein besonderer Fall hervorgehoben zu werden', matching the published §12/13.
